title: No Single Point
summary: Find the parts whose failure takes everything down, then remove them with redundancy, health checks, failover and multiple zones.

goals.text: Do availability math for series and parallel parts
Route around failures with health checks
Spread across zones and budget spare capacity

steps.title: One server, one database
body: Ledgerly sends invoices for 5,000 small businesses. It runs on one web server and one Postgres database. Both are solid machines that rarely fail.
“Rarely” adds up, though: each is down roughly half a percent of the time for crashes, patches and hardware swaps.

steps.title: When the only one breaks
body: At 02:10 the web server's disk fails. There's no other copy of it, so every customer gets an error until someone rebuilds it.
A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure alone stops the whole system. Ledgerly has two: the web server and the database.

card.title: Single point of failure
lines: the web server's disk dies at 02:10
no other machine can serve the site
# back when someone rebuilds it: ~3 h

steps.title: Counting nines
body: Availability is the share of time the system works. When a request needs every part in a chain, the availabilities multiply — two 99.5% parts give 99.0%.

AvailabilityDowntime
99%3.7 days down / year
99.9%8.8 hours
99.99%53 minutes
99.999%5 minutes

callout.text: In series, availability only goes down. In parallel — where any one copy is enough — it goes up fast.

steps.title: Two web servers and a balancer
body: Add a second web server and a load balancer. Now the web tier is only down if both servers are down at once: 0.5% × 0.5% = 0.0025% of the time.
But look at the score: the load balancer is a new SPOF and the database still is one. Overall availability is now capped by the weakest single part.

steps.title: Noticing a dead server
body: Redundancy only helps if traffic avoids the broken copy. The balancer runs health checks: it calls each server's /health every few seconds and removes one after several failures in a row.

A shallow check (“the process answers”) misses a server that can't reach its database. A deep check tests real dependencies — but keep it cheap, and don't let one shared dependency fail every server's check at once.

card.title: Health checks
lines: 3 failures in a row → out of rotation
= users never reach the dead server
# check what matters: can it reach the DB?

steps.title: A database waiting in the wings
body: Databases hold state, so you can't just run two independent ones. The common pattern is active–passive: a primary serves everything while a standby receives every change through replication and stays ready.
With synchronous replication a write is confirmed only once the standby has it too, so a failover loses nothing — at the cost of a little extra write latency.

card.title: Active–passive database
lines: primary takes all reads and writes
# standby waits, ready to take over

steps.title: Promoting the standby
body: The primary dies. Failover takes a few steps: notice (missed heartbeats), decide (promote the standby), redirect (move a virtual IP or DNS name so apps reconnect). The total is usually tens of seconds — far better than hours, but not zero.
Detection is the tricky part: a primary that's only slow or cut off might still be accepting writes. Before promoting, the old primary must be fenced off, or you get two primaries and a split brain.

card.title: Failover timeline
lines: 40 s  apps reconnect to the new address
= ~40 s of failed writes, not 3 hours
! fence the old primary: no split brain

steps.title: Everybody works
body: The web tier was already active–active: both servers take traffic, so losing one just means the other works harder — no switch-over. Do the same for the balancers: two of them, both published in DNS (or sharing a floating address).
Active–active suits stateless parts. For databases it means multiple writers and conflict resolution, so most teams keep their primary active–passive.

card.title: Active–active vs active–passive
lines: ! shared state must be safe to split
+ simple for databases, costs a failover

steps.title: Don't share a building
body: Every copy still sits in one data center. A power cut, cooling failure or fibre cut there takes all of them at once — they share a hidden SPOF.

Cloud regions are split into availability zones: separate buildings with independent power and network, a millisecond or two apart. Put one copy of each tier in each zone, and a whole zone can fail while the other carries on.
changes: ~ One copy of each tier per zone

card.title: Availability zones
lines: 1–2 ms apart: fast enough for sync copies
each zone has an LB, web and a database
= a whole building can go dark

steps.title: The survivor carries everyone
body: Zone B loses power. Health checks and DNS shift all traffic to zone A within seconds. The primary database already lives in zone A, so writes never stop; had it been in B, the standby in A would have been promoted.

The catch is capacity. Zone A must absorb the full load, so with two zones each must normally run at most half full. Three zones need only ⅔ — one reason many teams use three. Redundancy you can't afford to keep spare isn't redundancy.

steps.title: Assume every part will fail
body:
• A SPOF is anything whose failure alone stops the system — hunt for hidden shared ones too.
  • Series parts multiply availabilities down; parallel copies push them up.
  • Health checks turn redundancy into actual failure avoidance.
  • Stateless tiers go active–active; databases usually go active–passive with fenced failover.
  • Spread copies across zones and keep enough spare capacity to lose one.
